analytic.title: Real-Time Scheduling and Analysis of Synchronous OpenMP Task Systems with Tied Tasks *

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Synchronous parallel tasks are widely used in HPC for purchasing high average performance, but merely consider how to guarantee good timing predictabilities. OpenMP is a promising framework for multi-core real-time embedded systems. The synchronous OpenMP tasks are significantly more difficult to schedule and analyze due to constraints posed by OpenMP specifications. An important OpenMP feature is tied task, which must execute on the same thread during the whole life cycle. This paper designs a novel method, called group scheduling, to schedule synchronous OpenMP tasks, which divides tasks into several groups, and assigns some of them to dedicated cores, in order to isolate tied tasks. We derive a linear-time computable response time bound. Experiments with both randomly generated and realistic OpenMP tasks show that our new bound significantly outperforms the existing bound.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: To fully utilize the capacity of multi-cores, software must be parallelized. A widely-used paradigm to design parallel software operates on the principle of divide-and-conquer: a parent task distributes its work to child tasks, which are executed in parallel and merge their results once all completed. In real-time scheduling, such behavior is modeled as synchronous parallel tasks and motivates much theoretical work on their scheduling and analysis problems [1][2][3][4][5].

OpenMP [6] is the de facto parallel programming framework for shared memory architectures, which can greatly simplify the development of parallel software by providing various mechanisms to explore the explicit and implicit software parallelism. OpenMP is not only widely used in high-performance and general computing, but also drawing increasing attentions in the embedded and realtime computing domain [7][8][9][10][11][12]. In this paper, we focus on the real-time scheduling and analysis problem of synchronous parallel tasks realized in the OpenMP framework.

With OpenMP, one can design synchronous parallel tasks with either implicit tasks (e.g., using omp loop) or explicit tasks (using omp task). In either way, the tasks in OpenMP are by default tied, which requires the task to only execute on one working unit, called threads in OpenMP. during its life cycle without migrating to other working units. A task is allowed to migrate to other working units only if it is explicitly specified by the untied keyword when being created. In OpenMP, all tasks are tied by default because they enjoy the following benefits: (1) tied tasks preclude migrations among working units, which simplifies the scheduler and reduces context switch cost [8]; (2) tied tasks may automatically prevent deadlocks in the presence of critical sections in most cases [11].

However, the tied task feature raises significant challenges to real-time scheduling and analysis of OpenMP task systems. Serrano et al [8] showed that the existing scheduling algorithms BFS (breadth-first-scheduling) and WFS (work-first-scheduling) are both in general not work-conserving if the OpenMP task system contains tied tasks, and thus the timing analysis techniques (e.g., the classical response time bound [13]) for parallel task models based on the work-conserving properties are not applicable. Sun et al. [9] further showed that tied tasks may cause extremely bad timing behavior. In the worst case, the parallel workload of the whole task system is completely tied to a single core, where the benefit of using multi-core processors complete vanishes. Therefore, existing algorithms in OpenMP are indeed not suitable to real-time systems when guaranteed response time bounds are a major concern.

In this paper, we develop a new approach, group scheduling (GS), to schedule synchronous OpenMP task systems. GS divides tasks into groups, and assigns some groups to dedicated cores, in order to isolate tied tasks that interferes with each other and may harm the work-conserving property. We develop techniques to derive a sound bound for response time. To the best of our knowledge, the only existing work on real-time scheduling and analysis of OpenMP task systems with tied tasks is [9], which proposed a scheduling algorithm BFS * to mitigate the problem caused by tied tasks. While BFS * is applicable to any OpenMP task system, our new algorithm GS is designed specifically for synchronous OpenMP task system and guarantees tighter response time bound than BFS * . We conduct experiments with both random task models and workload generated by realistic OpenMP programs. Experiment results show that GS outperforms BFS * under different parameter settings.

div.head: GROUP SCHEDULING ALGORITHM
div.p: Our proposed group scheduling (GS) approach consists of the task grouping, offline task assignment and online scheduling phases:

• Task Grouping. In this phase, tasks are grouped together if they have the same ancestor (See in Sec. 3.1 for more precise). • Offline Task assignment. In this phase, we assign a subset of dedicated cores to a task group if it may have bad timing behavior due to interference of other task groups. Otherwise, we do not explicitly assign cores to a task group. • Online Scheduling. If a task group is assigned a set of cores, we schedule its tasks on these cores at runtime, which precludes the interference from any other task outside that task group. For the task groups that are not explicitly assigned cores in the offline task assignment phase, we schedule their tasks together on cores assigned to their common ancestor. Although the tied tasks of different groups may interfere with each other, we will design mechanisms to schedule them in a work-conserving way.

div.head: EVALUATION
div.p: For each task set, we calculate the response time bound for GS in (17), denoted by R д , and we compare it with the response time bound for BFS * in (12) of [9], denoted by R b .

div.head: Randomly Generated Tasks
div.p: We generate n tasks {τ 1 , • • • , τ n }, and each task is tied with p tied probability. The vertex of each task has an execution time ranging in [50, 100]. For any task τ i , the child tasks of τ i created by the same vertex are no more than Ψ. We conduct experiments with different combinations of parameters in Fig. 3. The values of the configurations are written in the figure caption. In Fig. 3, the normalized bound R д consistently outperforms the bound R b under different parameter settings. It indicates that our GS method can always improve the response time. The bound improvement becomes better as task number increases, and is slightly weak when the number of cores, the number of tied tasks and the number of child tasks created by the same vertex are large.

div.head: Realistic OpenMP Programs
div.p: We collect 11 OpenMP programs based on C language from several benchmarks that contain tied tasks and synchronization points (e.g.,taskwait), as shown in Table 1.

We obtain the task model of these benchmark programs by analyzing the code executed during runtime. We measure the execution time for vertices by executing the programs on hardware. We instrument the OpenMP programs with instructions reading the timer at the beginning and end of each vertex, and the execution time of the vertex is the difference between the two time stamps. Although this approach cannot provide safe WCET bounds, these reference Table 1: Summary of selected OpenMP programs benchmarks programs ompb [14] taskbench(th) dash [15] nbody_method(nd) ompmpi [16] pingpong(pg), overlap(op) bots [17] fft(ft), fib(fb), nqueens(ns), sort(st) alignment(at), sparselu(su), strassen(sn) WCET values give a rough idea of the workload of each vertex. Currently the reference values provided by this approach are obtained on an Intel i7-4770 CPU with 3.5GHZ and 8192KB cache size. As shown in Fig. 4, the bound R д is 36% better than R b on average for the programs in Table . 1 with core number m = 16. Especially for the programs "st" and "ns"in "bots" [17] that have deeply nested tied tasks, the bound is improved by GS algorithm more than 60%.

div.head: CONCLUSION
div.p: This paper proposes a group scheduling (GS) algorithm for synchronous OpenMP task systems, which divides tasks into groups and assigns some of them to dedicated cores, in order to preclude task interference that may damage timing predictability. We develop response time analysis under GS. Experiment results show that our response time bound significantly outperforms the existing bound.
